endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: determine whether there is a way for impacted individuals to provide timely feedback about whether they were satisfied with the care/service that was provided with input from an AI solution, and whether it is equally accessible to all relevant subgroups.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Is there a consistent, accessible mechanism for patients to ask questions or raise concerns about AI in their care at any point during their visit or episode?

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Assess the proportion of synthetic to non-synthetic training data and verify training data is not overly homogenous or GAI-produced to mitigate concerns of model collapse.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Set up communication channels with stakeholders

endorsements.title: Achieving health equity through conversational AI: A roadmap for design and implementation of inclusive chatbots in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Additionally, health chatbots should offer users an easy way to report safety concerns or file complaints.

endorsements.title: Patient Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging
endorsements.quote: Feedback mechanisms: develop channels for patients to provide feedback on their experiences with AI-driven diagnostics to help refine these systems and ensure they meet patient needs and expectations.

endorsements.title: Reframing Justice in Healthcare AI: An Ubuntu-Based Approach for Africa
endorsements.quote: The feedback channels allow patients and providers to report misdiagnoses or usability issues directly, so that AI tools evolve responsively to the real conditions of African clinical practice.

endorsements.title: Health Equity Considerations in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
endorsements.quote: Policy frameworks should also establish clear accountability mechanisms for failures of AI tools to perform as intended, including pathways for patients and health care professionals to report concerns about bias or inaccurate outputs.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether a patient feedback or reporting channel for AI-assisted care leads to more concerns being reported or addressed, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support for the practice rests on eight framework and commentary endorsements, one of which (NIST AI 600-1) addresses training data rather than patient feedback.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The eight sources are three frameworks, one consensus guideline, and four commentaries, and these reflect expert opinion rather than measured effects. The quoted NIST AI 600-1 text concerns synthetic training data and does not bear on patient reporting channels, so seven sources apply directly.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether a feedback mechanism is equally accessible to all relevant subgroups, and the conversational AI equity roadmap calls for an easy way to report safety concerns. Neither source reports data on whether such channels reach patients with limited English proficiency, low literacy, or Medicaid coverage.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide lists this practice at the must level, while the CHAI playbooks list it at the may level, and the remaining sources say should. These are voluntary frameworks. The Health Equity Considerations commentary calls on policy frameworks to create reporting pathways for bias or inaccurate outputs, which suggests such pathways are not yet a settled requirement.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare sites with and without a patient-facing AI feedback channel and measure the volume of concerns reported, time to response, the share of reports that lead to a change in the AI tool or care process, and patient-reported trust. Such studies would also need to establish how often AI-related harms currently go unreported.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two endorsing sources raise equal access across subgroups as a design goal, but health systems have no evidence on which channel formats these patients can use and would need to collect their own uptake data by language, literacy, and payer.
